slides: Open the lecture by separating the geometric problem from the numerical return value. A distance query is not just a scalar; it is a statement about which features are closest, which parameters were legal, and which constraints became active during minimization.

Set up the reusable data contract before any formula. The representation gives a parameter domain, the squared distance gives an objective, and the result must identify the closest feature. This contract will repeat for lines, rays, segments, polygons, curves, and GJK.

Use the table to show that line, ray, and segment queries are the same projection viewed through different legal domains. The expensive bug is usually not the dot product; it is forgetting which boundary case changed the minimizer.

This slide connects the formula to the notebook check. The example reports a legal segment parameter and a zero residual against the intended invariant. Ask students what the output should contain if the projection had landed beyond either endpoint.

Move from formulas to regions. For polygons, the question is which constraints are active at the minimizer. This is why closest-point code often looks like a decision tree: each branch is identifying a vertex, an edge, or an interior feature.

Present polylines and polygon boundaries as searches over simpler distance queries. The scalar distance is the easy aggregate. The useful graphics result is the winning segment or vertex, because later code needs a contact point, normal direction, or stable cache key.

Reframe the many line, ray, and segment combinations as one quadratic minimization over different product domains. Once students see the unit square picture, the long list of cases becomes active-set logic rather than a memorization exercise.

For curves, the mental model should stay the same even though the algebra changes. The residual vector at an interior closest point is perpendicular to the tangent. What changes is that the stationary equation may have several legal roots.

Use this slide to explain why convex distance algorithms care so much about the origin. The shape pair becomes one derived convex set. Intersecting the origin means overlap, while the closest point to the origin gives a separating vector.

Keep GJK concrete. The algorithm never needs to construct the entire Minkowski difference. It samples support points, keeps a simplex, and repeatedly asks whether that simplex proves intersection or supplies a closest direction back to the origin.

The diagnostic curve is useful because it exposes more than a final answer. The smooth middle reflects an interior projection, while the outer parts show boundary control. This picture helps students recognize when a derivative or normal jumps.

Stress that a production distance routine should return a certificate. The closest points, parameters, feature labels, and status flags are what make downstream debugging possible. Without them, correct distances can still produce unstable normals or broken caches.

Use this slide to slow down around robustness. A tolerance is not a magic eraser; it is a decision about which nearby geometric model the program will use. The returned status should make that decision visible during testing.

Summarize the implementation strategy as a loop. This is the practical payoff of the chapter: the programmer can approach many different primitives with the same sequence of representation, minimization, active-feature classification, return state, and verification.

Use the exercise to reverse the usual order. Students should first reason geometrically about the active feature, then decide which computations certify that choice. This prevents distance formulas from becoming uninspected black-box evaluations during implementation reviews.

Close by returning to the durable pattern. The chapter is not a pile of unrelated formulas; it is a family of constrained minimization problems. The implementation goal is a checked certificate that remains meaningful under perturbation, degeneracy, and downstream use.
